shortName: zColo, LLC v. Markley Boston, LLC
citation: zColo, LLC v. Markley Boston, LLC
forum: United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: zColo, LLC, a DataBank-owned colocation provider, sued its Boston landlord, Markley Group, over a lease at the One Summer Street carrier-hotel data center. zColo alleges Markley engaged in a years-long letter-writing campaign, refused to recognize the 2020 transfer of the lease from zColo's former parent Zayo, and demanded more than $70 million despite a monthly rent of about $63,700. It also alleges Markley refused to respond to remediation proposals and to recognize its right to extend the lease. Claims include breach of the lease, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and unfair and deceptive practices under Massachusetts law. zColo seeks a court interpretation of the lease and damages. Markley denies the allegations and said it would assert its own claims.

shortName: SS Penn, LLC v. North Beaver Township
citation: SS Penn, LLC v. N. Beaver Twp., No. 1406 C.D. 2026 (Pa. Commw. Ct.).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: A data center developer appealed a county court ruling to the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania. The developer is seeking to quash a municipal ordinance that it claims was put in place after it submitted a development plan for a data center. The ordinance in this case was established by North Beaver Township.

shortName: Bockrath v. Coweta Cnty.
citation: Bockrath v. Coweta Cnty.
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Ron Bockrath and other Coweta County, Georgia residents sued Coweta County over the county commission's approval of rezoning approximately 829 acres near Sargent Road and Wagers Mill Road from Rural Conservation to Industrial use for the proposed "Project Sail" data center campus (13 buildings, roughly 378,000 square feet each). Plaintiffs allege the county violated its own zoning procedures and comprehensive plan by approving industrial development on land designated for rural conservation, that commissioners engaged in improper ex parte communications with the developer, and that the environmental review understated impacts on wetlands and groundwater recharge areas. The petition seeks to void the rezoning decision.

shortName: Land Legacy, Inc. v. Ringle
citation: Land Legacy, Inc. v. Ringle, Alan J.
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Land Legacy, Inc., a conservation land trust, sued landowner Alan Ringle and his family, alleging that a 2013 conservation easement covering roughly 270 acres of a larger 800-plus-acre property near Sand Springs, Oklahoma — in exchange for which the Ringles reportedly received a $3.8 million tax deduction — permanently bars industrial development, including roads and buildings, on the land now proposed as the site for a large-scale Google data center ("Project Spring"). Land Legacy alleges the Ringle family knowingly proceeded with the data center plans in bad faith despite the restrictions, and that the easement was not disclosed during the project's rezoning application, which affirmatively denied the existence of any development restrictions on the property; the trust seeks to have the easement enforced and the rezoning process redone with its participation. The City of Sand Springs has stated it does not believe the lawsuit has merit or will affect the project's future.

shortName: In re Iris Energy Ltd. Securities Litigation
citation: In re Iris Energy Limited Securities Litigation
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Securities
summary: Investors led by Paul Williams-Israel filed a putative class-action securities-fraud lawsuit against Iris Energy Limited (NASDAQ: IREN), a Bitcoin-mining company that had pivoted toward marketing itself as a high-performance computing (HPC) data center operator, and several of its executives. Plaintiffs, representing purchasers of IREN securities between June 20, 2023 and July 11, 2024, allege the company made materially false and misleading statements overstating its Childress County, Texas facility's readiness for HPC workloads — including claims about backup power and cooling infrastructure — based substantially on a July 11, 2024 short-seller report by Culper Research, after which IREN's share price fell roughly 15%. The suit seeks damages under federal securities laws on behalf of the affected investor class; this litigation is separate from an earlier, unrelated 2022 securities suit concerning IREN's 2021 IPO disclosures, which a different judge dismissed without prejudice.

shortName: West Virginia-Citizen Action Group, Inc. v. Crowder
citation: West Virginia-Citizen Action Group, Inc. v. Laura M. Crowder, Director WV DEP
corporateEntities: Microsoft, Nuscale, Fidelis, Monarch Compute Campus
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: West Virginia Citizen Action Group appealed to the state Air Quality Board the Department of Environmental Protection's 2025 air permit for a biomass and carbon-capture facility near Point Pleasant, Mason County. The facility was planned by a Fidelis New Energy affiliate as part of the Monarch campus, a data center project. The group challenges the permit's issuance and has objected that the developer's counsel, the state House Speaker, has a conflict of interest. In May 2026 the permit holder told the DEP it was surrendering the permit because the project had shifted from the biomass plant toward establishing data centers.

shortName: Nat’l Ass’n for Advancement of Colored People-Chesterfield Branch v. State Corp. Comm’n
citation: Nat’l Ass’n for Advancement of Colored People-Chesterfield Branch v. State Corp. Comm’n, No. 260476 (Va. filed May 27, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The NAACP Chesterfield Branch appeals to the Supreme Court of Virginia from the State Corporation Commission proceeding, Case No. PUR-2025-00037. There, the State Corporation Commission approved the Dominion Energy’s Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center, a gas power plant. The appeal alleges violations of the Virginia State Air Pollution Control Law, the Virginia Administrative Process Act, the Virginia Environmental Justice Act, and the federal Clean Air Act.

shortName: In re Interstate Power & Light Co.
citation: In re Interstate Power & Light Co., Docket No. GCU-2026-0002 (Iowa Utils. Comm'n filed Apr. 29, 2026).
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: Interstate Power and Light (Alliant Energy) sought a certificate of public convenience from the Iowa Utilities Commission for a 720 MW gas plant called the Morgan Valley Energy Center. The plant is intended to meet demand from data centers, among other loads. Several objections have been loged in the docket based on transparency, air quality and siting concerns.

shortName: CAL Realty, LLC v. City of Gibraltar
citation: CAL Realty, LLC v. City of Gibraltar, 2:26-cv-12893, (E.D. Mich., filed Aug. 17, 2026)
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan
category: Constitutional Law: Due Process
secondaryCategory: Constitutional Law: Equal Protection

shortName: Hairston Clan v. Stokes Cnty.
citation: Hairston Clan v. Stokes Cnty.
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The National Hairston Clan, CleanAIRE NC, the Dan River Basin Association, 7 Directions of Service, and more than a dozen Walnut Cove-area residents sued Stokes County, North Carolina over the county commissioners' January 2026 rezoning votes (approved 3-2) that opened roughly 1,800 acres of land to industrial use for the "Project Delta" hyperscale data center. Plaintiffs allege the rezoning was approved without the procedural safeguards, factual analysis, and reasoned decision-making North Carolina law requires — including inadequate public notice and failure to meaningfully assess impacts on noise, air quality, water, and sites of cultural and historical significance to the Saura Tribe and descendants of formerly enslaved families (including the Hairston and Bailey families) who maintain cemeteries on and near the rezoned land. The suit asks the court to strike down both zoning actions; the county has since voted to restart the rezoning process for the project.

shortName: Independent Market Monitor for PJM v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
citation: Indep. Mkt. Monitor for PJM v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: Monitoring Analytics, PJM's independent market monitor (IMM), filed a complaint with FERC on November 25, 2025 raising concerns about the growing impact of data center and other large-load growth on PJM's capacity market, which the IMM's filing states fell short of meeting its reliability objective and reserve-margin target in the most recent capacity auction. The complaint centers on how new large loads — including those that do not commit to bringing their own new generation or agreeing to demand-response curtailment — should be treated for capacity-market purposes, building on the IMM's earlier position (raised in related PJM/FERC proceedings on data center co-location) that new large loads should generally be required to bring their own matching new generation; the complaint asks FERC to address the resulting reliability and cost-allocation risks.

shortName: Clean Air Coalition of Western New York, Inc. v. New York State Public Service Comm'n
citation: Matter of Clean Air Coalition of W. N.Y., Inc. v New York State Pub. Serv. Commn.
forum: "State of New York, Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Judicial Department"
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The Clean Air Coalition of Western New York and the Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice, sued the New York State Public Service Commission (PSC) over its approval allowing Digihost International, a Canadian cryptocurrency company, to acquire the Fortistar natural-gas power plant in North Tonawanda for 24/7 crypto-mining operations. Petitioners alleged the PSC failed to analyze the climate and environmental effects of the ownership transfer as required by New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, contending the plant — which had historically run intermittently for only 10 to 74 days a year — would see its greenhouse gas emissions increase by as much as 3,500% under continuous crypto-mining operation. A trial court initially dismissed the case, but the Appellate Division, Third Department reversed, holding that the petitioners' proximity to the facility gave them standing to challenge the increased use, and returned the case to the trial court to proceed on the merits.

shortName: In re Duke Energy Progress, LLC
citation: In the Matter of: Duke Energy Progress, LLC, and Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 2026 Solar Resource Procurement Request for Proposals for Solar and Solar
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: This proceeding concerns Duke Energy's annual competitive-bidding process for new solar and solar-plus-storage generation, required under North Carolina's 2021 clean-energy law, in a docket where Duke had proposed procuring 770 megawatts of solar for 2026 — short of the 1.7 gigawatts called for under its 2024 regulator-approved carbon-reduction plan, citing federal tax-credit changes. On April 23, 2026, North Carolina Utilities Commission Chair William Brawley issued an order (signed only by the Commission's chief clerk, without an apparent vote of the full panel) deferring Duke's 2026 solar and storage procurement entirely until the company's next carbon-reduction plan is approved by year-end. Clean-energy advocacy groups — including the Sierra Club, Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, and Vote Solar, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, along with the Carolinas Clean Energy Business Association — filed motions for reconsideration arguing the order was "arbitrary and capricious," issued without proper Commission process, and would create a solar generation shortfall in the early 2030s just as Duke projects steep demand growth from data centers.

shortName: Amazon Data Services Inc. v. Bd. of Supervisors of King George City
citation: Amazon Data Services Inc. v. Board Of Supervisors of King George City
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Amazon Data Services filed a petition in King George County Circuit Court seeking judicial review of the county Board of Zoning Appeals' March 25, 2025 decision, which upheld the zoning administrator's non-response to Amazon's request for a determination of vested rights in roughly 869 acres approved for a data center campus. Amazon argues the zoning administrator's response was both untimely under the state's 90-day statutory deadline and legally deficient for failing to issue required findings, and contends it holds vested rights based on prior rezoning, proffer amendments, a special exception amendment, and a comprehensive plan amendment, plus more than $168.8 million invested in the property. The petition asks the court to vacate the zoning administrator's determination and confirm Amazon's vested rights; the county's Board of Supervisors and Birchwood Power Partners were also served, though Amazon states it alleges no wrongdoing by Birchwood.

shortName: Twente v. City of Edgerton
citation: Twente v. City of Edgerton, No. JO-2026-002314 (Kan. Dist. Ct. Johnson Cnty. Aug. 28, 2026).

shortName: Haley v. X.AI Corp.
citation: Haley v. X.AI Corp.
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Jason Haley, Preston Herrington, and Taylor Logsdon filed a putative class-action lawsuit — on behalf of a class potentially including more than 10,000 residents of Southaven and Horn Lake, Mississippi — against X.AI Corp., SpaceX, and subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that gas-fired turbines powering xAI's "Colossus" AI data center campus (which grew from roughly 3 to 57 turbines in under a year) create a public and private nuisance through near-constant roaring, humming, and low-frequency vibrations audible and felt in nearby homes 24 hours a day. Plaintiffs assert claims for private nuisance, public nuisance, negligence, negligence per se, and negligent infliction of emotional distress, and seek damages for loss of use and enjoyment of property, diminished property values, and emotional distress, as well as injunctive relief requiring the defendants to abate the noise.

shortName: BCB Cheyenne LLC v. MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC
citation: BCB Cheyenne LLC v. MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC
forum: United States District Court for the District of Wyoming
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: BCB Cheyenne LLC (d/b/a Bison Blockchain) sued MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC and several related entities (including MineOne Partners, Terra Crypto, SonicHash, and Bit Origin) in federal court, alleging breach of contract, anticipatory repudiation, tortious interference with contractual relations, and related claims arising from a 2022 partnership to develop the North Range and Campstool Bitcoin mining/data center sites near Cheyenne. BCB alleges MineOne pushed it out as operator of both projects without cause and denied it the financial return from the ventures; defendants answered and asserted counterclaims against BCB. The case was terminated in the district court on October 15, 2024 and was subsequently appealed to the Tenth Circuit.

shortName: Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC
citation: Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Mary Ann Rizzo, owner of property across the street from Verizon's proposed $4 billion data center site in Somerset, New York, sued Verizon along with city, county, and state agencies in November 2010, alleging officials rushed through the project's tax-break approval process and failed to follow required due process. A Niagara County court ruled against Rizzo in January 2011; Rizzo appealed to the Appellate Division, Fourth Department, which rejected Verizon's request to expedite the appeal timetable, extending the case's briefing schedule while Verizon separately weighed an alternative data center site in Wyoming.

citation: In re Equinix Data Ctr. Approval (City of Cape Town Planning Appeals Auth. Sept. 14, 2026).

category: Other

shortName: Lingelbach v. Twiggs Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Lingelbach v. Twiggs County Board of Commissioners
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Twiggs County, Georgia resident Nancy Lingelbach and other residents (including plaintiff and attorney Rob Fricks) sued the Twiggs County Board of Commissioners over its mid-September 2025 approval of a roughly 300-acre data center project proposed by Eagle Rock Partners. Plaintiffs allege the rezoning public notice was improperly posted at the wrong location and that the process was rushed through to bypass Georgia's Development of Regional Impact (DRI) review — a state communication mechanism (not a regulatory approval tool) that was administratively paused at the time — meaning the project's specific square footage and water needs were never disclosed through that review as they otherwise would have been. The suit followed a contentious public hearing at which residents voiced opposition; the county has disputed the plaintiffs' characterization of the process in its formal response.

shortName: Dubose v. Cnty. of Imperial
citation: Tom Dubose et al vs. County of Imperial et al
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: Five Imperial County residents (Tom Dubose, Kevin Smith, Ryan Dickerson, Daryl Dickerson, and Carl Stills) petitioned for a writ of mandate, and for declaratory and injunctive relief, against the County of Imperial and its registrar of voters. They sought to keep the proposed "Imperial County Data Center Prohibition Act" off the ballot. Petitioners argue the initiative violates California's single-subject rule, improperly regulates administrative functions through the initiative process, contains unlawful retroactive provisions, and raises First Amendment and preemption problems. The measure's proponents were named as real parties in interest.

shortName: In re Application of Ohio Power Co.
citation: In re Application of Ohio Power Co.
corporateEntities: AEP, Stargate manufacturing and data center site in Lordstown, OH  (Softbank, Oracle, OpenAI partnership), The Ohio Manufacturers' Association Energy Group, Ohio Power Co.,
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: The Ohio Manufacturers' Association (OMA) is appealing to the Supreme Court of Ohio a Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) decision approving a new tariff proposed by American Electric Power (AEP) Ohio specifically for data centers and other large-load customers. AEP's tariff requires data center customers to commit to minimum purchase requirements (paying for at least 85% of their stated power needs even if actual usage is lower), 12-year minimum contracts, and exit fees, which AEP says are needed to prevent stranded infrastructure costs from being shifted to other ratepayers; OMA's appeal argues the tariff is unlawfully discriminatory against a specific customer class, that PUCO improperly sanctioned AEP's earlier unilateral moratorium on new data center service requests, and that AEP's underlying demand projections were unsubstantiated. AEP counters that the tariff protects existing customers, including manufacturers, from bearing infrastructure costs caused by data centers.

shortName: Matter of Sierra Club v City of N. Tonawanda
citation: Matter of Sierra Club v City of N. Tonawanda
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: This is a separate, related case from the PSC challenge above. The Sierra Club and three North Tonawanda residents petitioned to overturn the City of North Tonawanda Planning Board's local site plan approval allowing Digihost to install 14 shipping-container-sized structures housing cryptocurrency-mining computers on the grounds of the Fortistar power plant, alleging the Board violated the State Environmental Quality Review Act (SEQRA), the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, and local zoning and planning-review laws. State Supreme Court Justice Frank Sedita III dismissed the petition, ruling that the Sierra Club and residents — who alleged only that they lived "nearby" without specifying a distance or particularized harm — lacked standing, and that the petition was also untimely under the statutory filing deadline; the Fourth Department affirmed this dismissal.

shortName: Solar Energy Industries Association v. FERC
citation: Solar Energy Industries Assoc. v. FERC
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: A utility and a trade association representing electric utilities petitioned for review of a FERC order certifying Montana's Broadview Solar facility (a 160 MW solar array paired with a 50 MW battery, limited by inverters to 80 MW of AC output) as a "small power production facility" under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (PURPA), arguing its underlying DC generation and storage capacity exceeded PURPA's 80-megawatt qualifying-facility ceiling. On September 9, 2025, following a Supreme Court remand in light of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (which eliminated Chevron deference), the D.C. Circuit again affirmed FERC's position, holding that a facility's "power production capacity" is measured by its maximum net AC output to the grid — its "send-out capacity" — rather than the sum of its individual DC components.

shortName: Bluemile, Inc. v. Atlas Industrial Contractors, Ltd.
citation: Bluemile, Inc. v. Atlas Indus. Contrs., Ltd.
forum: "Court of Appeals of Ohio, Tenth Appellate District"
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: Bluemile, Inc., a Columbus, Ohio data center operator, sued Atlas Industrial Contractors after an Atlas employee performing electrical work at Bluemile's data center caused a power surge on February 10, 2011 that disrupted Bluemile's computer networking services and allegedly caused lingering equipment damage; Atlas filed a separate but related action against Bluemile. A related coverage dispute arose when Bluemile sought business-interruption insurance benefits from Hartford Casualty Insurance Company, which contested the scope of recovery under Bluemile's policy. On appeal, the Ohio Tenth District Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part a trial court ruling that had granted Bluemile partial summary judgment against Hartford and granted Atlas judgment notwithstanding the verdict against Bluemile.

shortName: Riera Graterol v. Allison-Smith Co. LLC
citation: Perpetio Riera Graterol, Noris Azuaje Montilla, et al. v. Allison-Smith Company LLC
category: Common Law: Torts
summary: The parents of Anthony J. Riera Azuaje, a 25-year-old subcontractor electrocuted on June 28, 2025 while working at the QTS data center construction site in Fayetteville, Georgia, sued electrical subcontractor Allison-Smith Company, alleging the company violated National Electrical Code standards and installed faulty electrical fittings that caused their son to contact an improperly grounded metal conduit, collapse from a scissor lift, and die four days later. Plaintiffs seek damages for their son's pain and suffering, funeral expenses, lost income, and punitive damages, arguing Allison-Smith showed "an entire want of care" for worker safety; QTS itself is not a named defendant in this suit.

shortName: Burke v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty.
citation: Katy Burke, et al. v. Board of County Supervisors of Prince William County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The American Battlefield Trust and ten landowners near the Manassas National Battlefield — including Katy and Liam Burke, who keep horses and donkeys on their farm near the site — sued the Prince William County Board of County Supervisors and Digital Gateway developers (including GW Acquisition Co. and H&H Capital Acquisitions), alleging the Board's December 2023 approval of three rezoning ordinances permitting roughly 23 million square feet of data centers on 2,100+ acres was void from the outset because the county's public notice advertising for the December 2023 hearing violated Virginia Code § 15.2-2204(A) and the county's own zoning ordinance. The Prince William Circuit Court initially sustained the Board's demurrer to this claim, but on March 31, 2026, the Virginia Court of Appeals — deciding this case jointly with a related suit, Oak Valley Homeowners Ass'n v. Board of County Supervisors — ruled that the trial court had erred and held that the same advertising deficiencies rendered the rezonings void ab initio, reinforcing an earlier ruling in the Oak Valley case that had already halted the Digital Gateway project.

shortName: Masaitis v. Coreweave, Inc.
citation: Masaitis v. Coreweave, Inc.
forum: United States District Court for the District of New Jersey
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Lobbying
summary: Lead plaintiff filed a putative securities class action against CoreWeave, Inc. and certain executives (CEO Michael Intrator, CFO Nitin Agrawal, and Chief Development Officer Brannin McBee), on behalf of investors who purchased CoreWeave stock between March 28, 2025 and December 15, 2025. The complaint alleges CoreWeave violated the Securities Exchange Act by overstating its ability to meet surging AI customer demand and materially understating the risk posed by its reliance on a single third-party data center supplier, Core Scientific — a risk that materialized when Core Scientific's shareholders rejected a planned all-stock merger with CoreWeave on October 30, 2025 (causing CoreWeave shares to fall more than 6%), and again in mid-December 2025 when further disclosures revealed weather-related construction delays at a Denton, Texas data center site and broader, earlier-known infrastructure setbacks. The suit seeks damages on behalf of the affected investor class under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act.

shortName: Havron v. City of Bessemer
citation: Havron v. City of Bessemer
corporateEntities: Logistics Land Investment, LLC; Hyperscale "Project Marvel"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: David Havron and other Bessemer, Alabama-area property owners near Rock Mountain Lake sued the City of Bessemer over its rezoning process for "Project Marvel," a proposed $14.5 billion, 18-building hyperscale data center campus (later reported to involve developer Logistics Land Investment LLC and QTS Data Centers) on roughly 700 acres of forested land. Plaintiffs' original April 2025 complaint alleged the city failed to provide adequate public notice before a scheduled rezoning vote; after the city restarted its rezoning process and the council granted final approval in November 2025, plaintiffs amended their complaint to argue the rezoning constituted arbitrary and capricious "spot zoning" unsupported by a rational basis, inconsistent with surrounding land uses, unsupported by any comprehensive plan, and unjustified by public necessity. The case included a discovery dispute over a subpoena to the developer that was briefly appealed via a mandamus petition; the parties ultimately filed a joint stipulation of dismissal with prejudice on June 22, 2026, ending the litigation.

shortName: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC v. United City of Yorkville
citation: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC, Chuck Kasper, et al. v. The United City of Yorkville, Illinois, Pioneer Development LLC, and Yorkville Nexus V LLC
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community LLC, along with individual residents and Skyfall Equestrian LLC, sued the City of Yorkville and developer Pioneer Development over the city's approval of the roughly 1,034-acre, 14-building "Project Cardinal" data center campus. Plaintiffs allege the city failed to properly notify nearby residents of the plans to annex unincorporated county land and rezone it for the project, and that required noise, traffic, and cooling-water-consumption impact studies were not adequately conducted before approval; they ask the court to void the underlying approvals. The parties have engaged in settlement discussions focused on revising the project's construction phasing order, with the developer intervening in the case as a defendant.

shortName: Valtrus v. Lumen
citation: Valtrus Innovations Ltd. v. Lumen Technologies, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-03928 (N.D. Ill. Apr. 8, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
category: Corporate: IP

shortName: Seidel v. Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC
citation: Corey Seidel, et al. vs. Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Twenty-two residents of Judson Township, North Dakota sued Atlas Power Holdings (operator of a Bitcoin-mining data center near Williston) and Williams County, alleging that persistent facility noise — measured by residents at 60 to 95+ decibels — constituted private and public nuisance and trespass, damaging their health, quality of life, and property values despite the installation of sound-mitigation walls. Plaintiffs also sought a writ of mandamus compelling Williams County to enforce its own zoning ordinance requiring that industrial noise and vibration be contained within the "Heavy Industrial" district, and asked the court to reverse what they alleged was an improper 2011 rezoning that permitted the facility's construction, along with at least $50,000 in damages. The court dismissed the trespass claim and both claims against Williams County in 2024, but let the nuisance and injunctive-relief claims against Atlas proceed; the parties reached a confidential settlement in mid-2025, with individual settlement agreements being finalized with residents into 2026.

shortName: Pearson v. Port of Morrow
citation: Pearson v. Port of Morrow
forum: United States District Court for the District of Oregon
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Michael Pearson and other Morrow and Umatilla County, Oregon residents — whose well water is contaminated with nitrates — sued the Port of Morrow, Amazon Data Services, and numerous other industrial defendants (including Lamb Weston, Madison Ranches, Threemile Canyon Farms, Portland General Electric, and Columbia River Processing), alleging the defendants' wastewater disposal practices contributed to unsafe nitrate levels in local groundwater. The complaint alleges that nitrate-laden wastewater from industrial food processors and data centers at the port — including water used to cool Amazon's servers, which becomes further concentrated with nitrates as it evaporates during cooling — is applied to area farmland in excess amounts, and seeks a court-ordered, state-backed groundwater remediation and monitoring program along with a program ensuring timely diagnosis and treatment of affected residents. In March 2026, Amazon agreed to pay $20.5 million to settle the claims against it without admitting liability, while plaintiffs' counsel stated they would continue litigating against the remaining defendants.

shortName: No Desert Data Center v. Pima Cnty.
citation: No Desert Data Center et al. v. Pima County et al.
forum: Superior Court of Arizona in Pima County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: The No Desert Data Center Coalition sued Pima County and its Planning and Zoning Commission over the county's rezoning of nearly 300 acres for the proposed "Project Blue" data center (developed by Beale Infrastructure), alleging the county violated Arizona's Open Meeting Law and deceived the public by failing to disclose in its rezoning agenda that the land was specifically intended for a data center, rather than for a broader range of possible uses. The complaint further alleges county staff secretly negotiated the sale of the land for over $20.8 million to an undisclosed buyer between 2023 and 2025, and asked the court to invalidate the rezoning. On April 11, 2026, Pima County Superior Court Judge Brenden Griffin dismissed the lawsuit, finding the county's failure to disclose the rezoning's specific purpose in its public agenda did not violate the Open Meeting Law; the coalition has stated it plans to appeal.

shortName: Mack Paramus Co. v. Mayor & Council of Borough of Paramus
citation: Mack Paramus Co. v. Mayor & Council of Borough of Paramus
forum: "Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Bergen County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions

shortName: Crosby v. Colleton Cnty.
citation: Miles Crosby, et al v. Colleton County
forum: Colleton County Court of Common Pleas
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Colleton County, South Carolina residents Miles Crosby and Jennifer Singleton, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, sued Colleton County to challenge a newly passed zoning ordinance allowing data centers to be built in rural areas of the county via a "special exception" permit. Plaintiffs allege the ordinance violates South Carolina zoning law, the county's own comprehensive plan, and its zoning code; the suit was filed shortly after developer Eagle Rock Partners applied under the new ordinance to build an 859-acre, 1,000-megawatt data center complex — potentially one of the largest in the country — within the ACE Basin, a 1.7-million-acre, largely undeveloped watershed around the Ashepoo, Combahee, and Edisto rivers. Plaintiffs argue the project would harm the area's rural character, dark night skies, water quality, and wildlife, and ask the court to invalidate the ordinance.

shortName: Application of Entergy Texas, Inc. to Amend Its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity
citation: Application of Entergy Texas, Inc. to Amend Its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity, Docket No. 56693 (Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. June 3, 2024).
category: Energy Law: State PUC

shortName: Caruthers v. Sangamon Cnty.
citation: Caruthers v. Sangamon County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Herschel Caruthers II, Linda M. Caruthers, and several other Waverly, Illinois-area residents and a kennel business owner sued Sangamon County, the Sangamon County Board, and C1 Sangamon (an entity affiliated with data center developer CyrusOne) to overturn the county board's April 7, 2026 approval of a conditional use permit for a roughly 280-acre, four-building data center on agricultural land in Talkington Township. Plaintiffs allege, across five counts, that the approving resolution was misdated to obscure a procedural defect, that the county failed to adequately study the project's impacts (including noise affecting a neighboring farmstead), and that the county should have required rezoning rather than a conditional use permit for a project of this scale. The suit asks the court to declare the county's approval invalid and to enjoin the county from issuing related building permits.

shortName: Stines et al v. PrimeBlock Operations, LLC et al
citation: Stines et al v. PrimeBlock Operations, LLC et al
forum: United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Murphy, North Carolina residents Judith Stines and William Huffman filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against California-based Bitcoin-mining company PrimeBlock, its affiliate Exponential Digital LLC (formerly Ankr Mining Solutions), and contractor Innotech Z Inc., alleging that a cryptocurrency-mining and AI data center operating since mid-2021 emits unrelenting noise from its servers, generators, and cooling systems — reaching as high as 90 decibels — that has "shattered" the rural community's quality of life and diminished property values for an estimated 1,000 property owners within a two-mile radius. Plaintiffs assert claims for private and public nuisance, negligence, gross negligence, and willful or wanton conduct, alleging the operators have refused to invest in basic noise-abatement measures such as soundproof barriers or vibration-dampening equipment, and seek both compensatory and punitive damages on behalf of the proposed class.

shortName: State ex rel. Mayes v. Arizona Corp. Comm'n
citation: State ex rel. Mayes v. Arizona Corporation Commission
forum: Superior Court of Arizona in Maricopa County
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes is challenging the Arizona Corporation Commission's December 10, 2025 approval (by a 4-1 vote) of a private energy agreement between Tucson Electric Power and Beale Infrastructure/Humphrey's Peak Power LLC to supply roughly 286 megawatts of electricity to the "Project Blue" hyperscale data center complex near Tucson. Mayes argues the agreement unlawfully allows TEP and the data center customer to set their own electricity rates by "mutual agreement," without requiring Commission review or approval of any future rate changes, and that this delegation of ratemaking authority to private parties violates Article 15, Section 3 of the Arizona Constitution, which vests ratemaking authority exclusively in the Commission. Mayes is seeking to have the Commission's approval vacated and the matter reheard with the unlawful rate-setting provision stricken, and has requested full party status for the State and the City of Tucson, including discovery, evidentiary hearings, and cross-examination rights.

shortName: Tonawanda Seneca Nation v. Genesee Cnty. Industrial Development Agency
citation: Tonawanda Seneca Nation et al v. Genesee County Industrial Development Agency d/b/a Genesee County Economic Development Center et al
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club filed an Article 78 petition in July 2025 against the Genesee County Economic Development Center, Stream U.S. Data Centers, and the Town of Alabama. They challenged two agency resolutions that granted about $472 million in subsidies for a data center at the STAMP industrial park. Petitioners alleged violations of New York's State Environmental Quality Review Act, arguing the review relied on general concepts rather than project specifics and was not coordinated with the town's site plan process. They asked the court to vacate the approvals, order a new review, and issue a temporary restraining order. In September 2025 the agency rescinded the approvals after Stream signaled it would expand the project, and petitioners moved to dismiss the case in October 2025.

shortName: Mountrail-Williams Electric Cooperative v. Williams Cnty.
citation: Mountrail-Williams Electric Cooperative v. Williams County, North Dakota
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: After Williams County commissioners voted on June 20, 2023 to order Mountrail-Williams Electric Cooperative (MWEC) to cut power to a Bitcoin-mining data center under construction by AtlasPower/FX Solutions — citing the developer's failure to meet county compliance requirements after an earlier shutdown order had been appealed and upheld — MWEC refused to comply and instead sought a court determination on the proper legal process for disconnecting a member's service. MWEC, a member-owned electric cooperative, stated it took its obligation to serve members seriously and would not unilaterally cut power without judicial guidance on whether the county's order was itself lawful and enforceable against the utility.

shortName: Center for Biological Diversity v. City of Pittsburg
citation: Center for Biological Diversity v. City of Pittsburg
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The Center for Biological Diversity petitioned for a writ of mandate against the City of Pittsburg, California under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), challenging the City Council's November 4, 2024 certification of an environmental impact report and approval of the Pittsburg Technology Park Specific Plan — a 76.38-acre, three-phase development including a roughly 368,551-square-foot data center on former golf course land containing grassland and wetlands habitat. The Center alleged the EIR failed to adequately disclose or analyze greenhouse gas emissions, water supply and quality, wildfire, traffic, noise, and biological resource impacts, and failed to adopt feasible mitigation measures or consider reasonable alternatives. On December 11, 2025, the parties (the Center, the City, and real parties in interest Pittsburg Data Hub, LLC and AVAIO Digital Partners) agreed to a settlement incorporating enhanced mitigation measures — including a 100%-renewable-energy commitment, rooftop solar, EV charging infrastructure, recycled water for cooling, and a $750,000 developer payment to a climate-resiliency fund — and stayed the litigation pending compliance.

forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: This is the appellate stage of the BladeRoom/Facebook/Emerson trade-secret dispute (previously summarized). After a jury found Emerson liable for breach of a non-disclosure agreement and willful and malicious misappropriation of BladeRoom's data center design trade secrets — awarding $10 million in lost profits and $20 million in unjust enrichment, later increased with punitive damages to roughly $60+ million — Emerson appealed to the Ninth Circuit. On August 30, 2021, the Ninth Circuit held that the district court misapplied English law in construing the NDA's two-year expiration clause, vacated the judgment, and remanded for a new trial to determine which disclosures occurred before versus after the NDA's termination date.

shortName: City of Sulphur Springs v. Luminant Mining Co., LLC
citation: City of Sulphur Springs vs. Luminant Mining Company, LLC, Luminant Generation Company, LLC, Vistra Corp., and Matthew Goering
forum: Court of Appeals for the Sixth District of Texas
category: Common Law: Property
summary: The City of Sulphur Springs sued former landowner Vistra Corp. and its subsidiaries Luminant Mining Company and Luminant Generation Company (along with an individual, Matthew Goering) over a deed restriction on land Vistra donated to the city in 2019 during its bankruptcy, which the city alleges was deceptively worded and now improperly bars the "commercial production, generation, or storage of electricity" needed to power a proposed 3,000-megawatt AI data center. The city contends Vistra falsely represented to regulators and the public that it held no rights over the land while secretly preserving the restriction to extract concessions once the data center project became viable. Vistra counter-sued, arguing the recorded land-use covenant is enforceable as written and that the city is trying to escape a bargain it accepted in 2019; the Texas Attorney General's Office has filed a brief supporting the city, arguing Luminant has used similar deed restrictions on other properties to entrench a potential energy monopoly.

shortName: Doyle v. An Bord Pleanála
citation: Doyle & Ors v An Bord Pleanála & Ors
category: Other
summary: Colin Doyle, Friends of the Irish Environment CLG, Futureproof Clare, Martin Knox, and Christine Sharp sought judicial review of two planning permissions granted by An Bord Pleanála (Ireland's national planning appeals board) in April 2024 for a large data center and substation development near Ennis, County Clare — comprising six two-story data halls (over 118,000 square meters) powered partly by 66 diesel generators and a 120MW gas facility, plus a new 110kV substation. Applicants raised six grounds for review, most concerning the development's climate impacts and alleged failure to comply with Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act, as well as a factual error in the Board's Environmental Impact Assessment regarding a Leisler's bat roost on the site (which the Board conceded was an error). On March 21, 2025, the High Court (Mr. Justice Richard Humphreys) dismissed the judicial review, finding the bat-related error was "harmless" and rejecting the broader climate and procedural grounds, thereby allowing the roughly €1.2 billion project to proceed.

citation: Oklo Inc. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL26-101-000 (FERC Aug. 28, 2026).
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: Oklo proposed a hybrid power plant consisting of a combination of advanced nuclear, fuel cells and gas generation to the PJM interconnection queue. PJM dropped the project from the current interconnection study cycle and Oklo petitioned FERC to undo PJM's decision. FERC's ruling sided with PJM because PJM followed its tariff and Oklo failed to remedy identified errors in its application.

shortName: Guido v. Columbia Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Gregory Guido, Jr. v. Columbia County Board Of Commissioners
corporateEntities: White Oak Business Center; Pumpkin Center
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Gregory Paul Guido Jr., a Harlem, Georgia resident, filed petitions for judicial review challenging the Columbia County Board of Commissioners' February 2026 approvals rezoning the White Oak Business Center and Pumpkin Center properties to Data Center District zoning for two large data center campuses. Guido alleges the county approved the rezonings without a verified water-usage or sewer-capacity analysis required by the county's Water and Sewer Division, relied on a stale traffic study prepared for an earlier version of the White Oak project, and failed to analyze the impacts of shifting the project's primary access point. The Superior Court dismissed all of Guido's related petitions (including a separate one concerning a nearby quarry) with prejudice; Guido moved for reconsideration, arguing the dismissal order failed to address the facts pled, improperly treated the distinct cases as one, and wrongly required land ownership (rather than proximity and demonstrable harm, which he argues is the correct standard under Georgia law) to establish standing. The matter is now before the Georgia Court of Appeals.

citation: Beaver Ventures LLC v. Washington County Assessor, TC-MD 240646N, 2026 WL 221842, at *1 (Or. Tax M. Div. Jan. 27, 2026).

summary: Beaver Ventures LLC — an entity affiliated with Digital Realty Trust — challenged the Washington County Assessor's denial of a property tax exemption sought for a Hillsboro, Oregon data center facility, reportedly valued at approximately $3.4 million in tax relief for the 2024–2025 tax year. A decision was issued in the matter; press coverage reports that Digital Realty's exemption request was rejected because the company had improperly attempted to combine two separate exemption applications into one filing.

shortName: Illinois Commerce Comm'n v. Commonwealth Edison Co.
citation: Illinois Commerce Commission On Its Own Motion v. Commonwealth Edison Company
corporateEntities: Commonwealth Edison Company; Illinois Commerce Commission; large-demand project applicants/customers, including data centers.
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: This is a Commission-initiated regulatory investigation rather than adversarial litigation. Following its March 20, 2026 approval of revised ComEd tariffs allowing larger security deposits from "Large Demand Project Applicants or Customers" (LDPACs, i.e., data centers) to protect against costs from canceled or abandoned projects, the Illinois Commerce Commission opened a broader investigation — reflecting ComEd's disclosure that it has 75 pending large-load applications collectively requesting more than 28,000 megawatts, exceeding the utility's all-time peak demand of roughly 24,000 megawatts — into what additional protections, exemptions, or tariff modifications may be needed to shield existing ratepayers from the costs of connecting data centers to the grid. Consumer and environmental advocacy groups are participating in the proceeding and have urged the Commission to consider requiring data centers to bear the full cost of dedicated infrastructure and to adopt incentives for developers that bring their own new clean-energy generation.

summary: CoreSite sued Fairfax County after the county's tax department repeatedly demanded that CoreSite disclose the identities and contact information of roughly 300 tenants at its four data centers and office building in Reston, Virginia, citing a Virginia Code provision allowing tax commissioners to require information relevant to assessing tax liability. CoreSite argues the county's demands were not reasonably specific to identifying Virginia taxpayers, were unduly burdensome, and risked exposing the company to liability from tenants whose contracts require confidentiality, since not all information requested was shown to relate to actual tax obligations. CoreSite asked the court to relieve it of the obligation to comply with the demands and to bar the county from taking adverse action — including threatened criminal penalties for noncompliance — while the dispute is resolved.

shortName: Montgomery v. DataOne USA LLC
citation: Montgomery v. DataOne USA LLC
forum: United States District Court for the District of New Jersey
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Two Vineland, New Jersey residents filed a putative class-action lawsuit against DataOne USA LLC, alleging that noise from DataOne's roughly 2.6-million-square-foot AI data center campus — including diesel generators, HVAC chillers, cooling towers, and condenser fans — constitutes a nuisance affecting approximately 1,000 residential properties within a mile of the facility. Plaintiffs, represented by Liddle Sheets, P.C. and Cohen & Riechelson, allege the persistent industrial noise (described by one plaintiff as sounding like "a helicopter hovering" or airport noise) has deprived residents of the use and enjoyment of their property and diminished property values; this was one of several similar noise-nuisance suits the same law firm filed against data centers nationwide the same week.

summary: The New Mexico State Ethics Commission sued Elevate New Mexico, an anonymous out-of-state entity behind a large physical- and digital-ad campaign urging New Mexicans to support the "Project Jupiter" data center complex, alleging the group violated the state Lobbyist Regulation Act by spending at least $2,500 to lobby the New Mexico Environment Department to approve air-quality permits for natural gas plants tied to the project without registering as a lobbyist organization. The Commission asks the court to require Elevate to register its campaign as lobbying activity and disclose its contributors, including names, addresses, and employers, arguing New Mexicans have a right to know who is funding efforts to influence official state actions affecting their communities.

They challenge the commissioners' February 2025 rezoning of roughly 390 acres from agricultural use to a planned unit development for "Project Louie," a data center later identified as Google's. Petitioners argue the rezoning was arbitrary, disregarded the county's comprehensive plan, and would harm property values, and they seek to halt the project. Construction has continued while the case is pending, and the plaintiffs recently moved for summary judgment.

CyrusOne, which had separately obtained a special use permit and variance in 2017 to build its own 350-foot tower for the same campus, alleged the Scientel tower would physically obstruct and interfere with wireless communications reaching CyrusOne's facility from the east and cause frequency congestion, and it sought a preliminary injunction to block Scientel's tower. The district court granted the defendants' motions to dismiss in part in July 2018 and later denied CyrusOne's preliminary injunction motion in March 2019; the parties ultimately settled the dispute through mediation, with the settlement terms undisclosed.

On June 18, 2026, Circuit Court Judge James A. Bonifant ruled that a county ordinance establishing a zoning map is not a "law" subject to referendum under the Frederick County Charter, and separately held the referendum petition itself was legally defective because its accompanying zoning maps were printed in black and white rather than the multi-color original, rendering them unreadable to voters. GWA alleged the sellers wrongly refused to approve "proffers" needed for GWA's rezoning application and/or sought to terminate the agreements to obtain a higher price, jeopardizing the entire rezoning effort; GWA sought a preliminary injunction and damages, including recovery of legal costs it says it was owed from a related prior dispute with Pageland. shortName: FLX Strong v. Town of Lansing Zoning Bd. of Appeals
citation: In re FLX Strong v. Town of Lansing Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 2026 N.Y. Slip Op. 76311(U) (N.Y. App. Div. 3d Dep’t Sept. 8, 2026).
forum: "State of New York, Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Judicial Department"
corporateEntities: TeraWulf, Inc., Lake Hawkeye, LLC; Cuyahoga Operating Co., LLC
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary:
The Appellate Court denied a motion to appeal a decision by a lower court. The decision sought for appeal was a claim brought by FLX Strong and CLEAN., two grassroots organization seeking to challenge the decision by the Lansing Town Zoning Board that the former site of a power plant classified for Industrial/Research use could be repurposed for a data center. The previous ruling is entered as an exhibit in the appeal filings.

In the previous ruling, the Zoning Board (and the developers) sought to dismiss the claim on the basis that the plaintiffs (FLX Strong et al.) lacked standing to bring a suit in the matter of the data center zoning, and that the case was not ripe because future zoning decisions could ameliorate their concerns. The lower court ruled that the plaintiffs did have standing because the organization members would have their enjoyment of the surrounding nature disturbed and also have noise impacts. It ruled that the case was ripe and that the plaintiffs stated a claim for relief, because they challenged the Zoning Board’s decision which permitted the project to proceed without additional approval for a first time use variance. 

The lower court denied the motion to dismiss the claim, and the Appellate Court denied the subsequent motion for an appeal. Upon the dismissal of the appeal, there have been no further updates on this case as of October 22nd, although the Lansing Town and the State of New York are considering bans on data center development.

shortName: King Sykes LLC v. City of Chicago
citation: King Sykes LLC v. The City of Chicago
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
category: Constitutional Law: Takings
summary: King Sykes LLC, owner of the vacant former Sykes Center site on Chicago's South Side, sued the City of Chicago and developer Scott Goodman, alleging the city and Goodman conspired to block a 2020–2021 deal to sell the 6.5-acre property to Equinix for $30 million to build a data center, in order to devalue the land so the city-Goodman "Bronzeville Lakefront" joint venture could later acquire it more cheaply. The complaint alleges city officials, including 4th Ward Alderwoman Sophia King, told Equinix the city would never approve a data center on the King Sykes site but would readily approve one on a nearby city-owned parcel (part of the former Michael Reese Hospital site) instead, causing Equinix to abandon its deal with King Sykes; the plaintiffs allege tortious interference with prospective economic advantage and sought $45 million in damages.

shortName: Scranton v. Ransom
citation: Scranton v. Ransom, No. 2026-01296 (Pa. Comm. Pleas Ct. filed Mar. 02, 2026)
forum: "Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Scranton Materials LLC, a stone-quarry owner, filed a curative-amendment land use appeal against the Ransom Township Board of Supervisors, arguing the township's zoning ordinance unlawfully excludes data centers as a permitted use anywhere within its borders, contrary to Pennsylvania law requiring municipalities to accommodate every lawful land use somewhere in their jurisdiction. The appeal followed the Board's January 20, 2026 vote (2-1) to dismiss Scranton Materials' proposed zoning overlay — which would have permitted a six-building, 251-acre data center campus on the company's Newton Road property — for lack of supporting testimony and evidence; the appeal alleges the Board abused its discretion and committed legal error, and asks the court to declare the ordinance exclusionary and permit the proposed development.

citation: Caparoula v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty., No. 1137-24-4 (Va. Cnty. Ct. 2024), aff’d, 2025 WL 2649495, No. 1042-25-3 (Va. Ct. App. 2025)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: William Caparoula and several neighboring property owners appealed the Prince William County Board of Supervisors' approval of Ordinance No. 23-52, which rezoned approximately 270 acres from a "Planned Mixed Residential" designation to a light-industrial district permitting data center use (the "Devlin" data center project), naming the Board and developer Stanley Martin Homes, LLC as appellees. Appellants argued the rezoning was arbitrary and capricious and constituted illegal spot zoning. On September 16, 2025, the Virginia Court of Appeals affirmed the rezoning, holding that the Board's decision met the "fairly debatable" standard, was not arbitrary and capricious, and did not constitute illegal spot zoning.

Petitioners are appealing the trial court's ruling that the county's failure to disclose the rezoning's data-center-specific purpose in its public hearing agenda did not violate Arizona's Open Meeting Law, seeking to have the appellate court overturn that determination and invalidate the rezoning of nearly 300 acres.

NV Energy argues that ratemaking and capacity-allocation authority cannot be delegated to a private arbitration process and must go through the PUCN. shortName: Blackboard Inc. v. International Business Machines Corp.
citation: Blackboard Inc. v. International Business Machines Corporation
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of New York
category: Arbitration
summary: This federal case was a petition to vacate or modify an American Arbitration Association award, not a new lawsuit on the merits. Blackboard Inc. petitioned the court to vacate or modify in part an arbitration award that had found in IBM's favor on IBM's counterclaims arising from a professional services agreement governing data center operations and cloud migration — with the arbitration tribunal finding Blackboard had improperly withheld payment. In a June 2, 2022 Opinion and Order, the district court denied Blackboard's petition to vacate and confirmed the award in IBM's favor, entering judgment for $26,650,148 on one counterclaim and $3,143,101 on a second, plus interest, while denying IBM's request for attorney fees.

summary: Four Goochland County, Virginia property owners — Cynthia Haas, Peggy Knisley, Virginia H. Reed, and Gail A. Minnick — sued Goochland County, its Board of Supervisors, and its Planning Commission, seeking to void the county's November 2025 approval (by a 4-1 vote) of a Technology Overlay District (TOD) and Technology Zone spanning about five miles along Route 288 in eastern Goochland, which would allow data centers and other high-tech uses near existing neighborhoods. Plaintiffs allege the county violated Virginia law governing zoning notice and process — including that the county's published notices were "wholly inadequate" and "confusingly defective," and that the version of the TOD ultimately adopted differed materially from what was described in the public notices, with late amendments introduced the night of the vote without further public input. The case remains in discovery over which of roughly 8,500 county documents must be produced; no trial date has been set.

citation: Ohio Environmental Council, et al., v. The State of Ohio
forum: Franklin County Court of Common Pleas
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The Ohio Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and individual plaintiffs (including Middletown resident Donna Ballinger) sued the State of Ohio and Ohio EPA, alleging the legislature violated the Ohio Constitution's single-subject rule by including provisions in the 2025 state budget bill that direct Ohio EPA to remove a 50-year-old "air nuisance" rule — which lets citizens sue major air polluters under the federal Clean Air Act — and that disqualify community air-monitoring data from use in state and local regulatory enforcement actions. Plaintiffs argue these substantive policy changes were improperly buried within an unrelated appropriations bill without adequate public notice, undermining protections for residents near industrial facilities; the case is pending before a judge in Franklin County without a live trial.

shortName: In re Wisconsin Power & Light Co.
citation: Application of Wisconsin Power and Light Company for Approval of an Individual Contract Rate Service Agreement for a Large Load Customer in Beaver Dam, Dodge County, Wisconsin
corporateEntities: Meta, Alliant Energy, Wisconsin Power & Light
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: This is a regulatory tariff proceeding rather than adversarial litigation. Alliant Energy (operating as Wisconsin Power and Light Company) applied to the Wisconsin Public Service Commission in April 2025 for approval of an Electric Service Agreement to serve a Meta data center in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, under the utility's existing Individual Contract Rate tariff. Following a public comment period — extended after the Commission's administrative law judge ordered Alliant to refile the application with fewer redactions — the Commission approved a modified agreement on May 7, 2026, that strengthened termination-charge protections for existing customers, added reporting and financial-safeguard requirements, required the data center customer to contribute to state energy-efficiency programs, and directed Alliant to file a separate standardized large-load tariff for future data center customers.

shortName: Henrico 183 LLC v. DeKalb County
citation: Henrico 183 LLC v. DeKalb County , No. 26CV7218 (Ga. Super. Ct. DeKalb Cnty. Aug. 5, 2026)
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Dekalb County is being sued by a data center developer over its temporary moratorium for data center permits. The developer claims they received assurances of approval from the county. Originially the project was proposed as a film studio in 2022. The County claims a moratorium is not a final decision and the plaintiffs missed a 12-month deadline to file their claims.

shortName: City of Hilliard v. Logue
citation: The City of Hilliard Ohio v. John Logue, Director, Ohio Environmental Protection Agency
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The City of Hilliard, Ohio appealed to the Environmental Review Appeals Commission a permit issued by the Ohio EPA for an AEP Ohio subsidiary to build 228 natural gas fuel cells, about 73 megawatts, to power an Amazon Web Services data center campus. The city argues the agency failed to give the local government notice before issuing the air permit, which allows up to 1.45 million pounds of carbon dioxide emissions per day. Hilliard turned to this appeal after learning that state law gives the state, not the city, authority over power siting, so its earlier attempt to block the project through rezoning failed. A resident has joined the appeal as a party, and it remains pending.

forum: Court of Appeals for the Fourteenth District of Texas

shortName: State ex rel. K-Nova II, LLC v. Village of Commercial Point
citation: The State of Ohio ex rel. K-Nova II, LLC v. Vill. of Com. Point., No. 2026-0694 (Ohio filed June 3, 2026)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: K-Nova II, LLC filed a verified petition in June 2026 seeking an expedited writ of mandamus compelling the Village of Commercial Point, its officials, and council members to vote on its major site plan application for a data center. It contends the council had to act within 60 days, but instead passed an 18-month moratorium on May 4, 2026 and tried to refund the fee. K-Nova argues its rights vested when it applied and that a retroactive moratorium cannot excuse the village from reviewing the plan.

shortName: Paulus v. Citicorp North America, Inc.
citation: Paulus v. Citicorp North America, Inc.
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio

summary: Delaware County, Ohio homeowner Kurt Paulus and his wife sued Citicorp North America, Citigroup Inc., and Citigroup Technology, alleging that generator noise from Citicorp's data center near U.S. Route 23 — which Paulus documented by tracking activation times and recording decibel levels from his bedroom — disrupted sleep and enjoyment of his property in a previously quiet, wooded residential area. Paulus, an engineer, stated he sought to resolve the issue directly with the company before filing suit, noting that Ohio law leaves townships without authority to regulate noise from commercial or industrially zoned property.

shortName: In re Virginia Electric & Power Co.
citation: Virginia Electric and Power Company - For approval and certification of electric transmission facilities: 500 kV and 230 kV Golden-Mars Lines, Lockridge 230 kV Loop, Sojourner 230 and Related Projects (Route 3A)
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: Dominion Energy applied to the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) for approval of new 500 kV and 230 kV transmission lines through eastern Loudoun County. The lines are part of a "reliability loop" intended to bring more power to the Ashburn data center cluster. In April 2026 the SCC found the project in the public interest and rejected undergrounding. It preferred a route that would cross school property, but the Loudoun County School Board declined to grant the needed easements. The SCC then approved an alternative overland route (Route 3A) in a June 29 final order. The Loudoun Valley Estates HOA, Loudoun County, and the School Board sought reconsideration, citing a new state law authorizing underground 500 kV pilot projects and disputing the route. On July 20, 2026 the SCC declined to suspend its order or reopen the record and dismissed the case. The School Board and a homeowner are preparing appeals to the Supreme Court of Virginia

shortName: Valenzuela v. Alliance Cloud Services, LLC
citation: Valenzuela et al v. Alliance Cloud Services, LLC
forum: United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Dowagiac, Michigan residents Lindy Valenzuela and John Valdes filed a proposed class action in May 2026 against Alliance Cloud Services, LLC, a subsidiary of Hyperscale Data, Inc., which operates a roughly 30-megawatt data center that has run since 2022 and is shifting from Bitcoin mining toward AI workloads. Plaintiffs allege the facility emits constant, high-pitched noise around the clock that has kept them from using their yards and homes. They contend the operator failed to install adequate soundproofing, and they assert a private nuisance claim. They seek damages and injunctive relief for owners and renters living within one mile of the facility. The city has a noise ordinance limiting sound to 65 decibels by day and 55 at night, which the plaintiffs cite, and the company has disputed the city's measurement methods.

shortName: Intergate Quincy II LLC v. Grant Cnty.

category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Intergate Quincy (a Sabey Data Centers entity) sued Grant County, Washington over property tax assessments on its Quincy data center campus, alleging the county assessor overvalued the property — assessing it at $239 million in 2020 and $237 million in 2021, versus the roughly $132 million and $123 million the company contends the property was actually worth. Intergate Quincy states it paid approximately $3.3 million in county taxes under protest over the relevant period, representing nearly $2 million it now seeks refunded as excess charges resulting from the allegedly inflated valuation. This was not the first such dispute in Grant County — the county was previously sued by another data center operator, H5 Data Centers, over a similarly contested assessment in 2019.

shortName: McDavid v. Scioto Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs
citation: McDavid v. Scioto Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs, No. 26CIH00167 (Scioto Cnty. Ct. Com. Pl. filed Feb. 18, 2026).

corporateEntities: Project Dazzler; Tilted Gate, LLC; Google
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Scioto County, Ohio resident Patrick McDavid sued the Scioto County Board of County Commissioners, alleging violations of Ohio's Open Meetings Act ("Sunshine Law") in connection with the board's negotiation of a Community Reinvestment Area tax agreement tied to a proposed Google data center campus. McDavid alleges the commissioners improperly conducted public business in closed-door executive sessions and failed to comply with state transparency requirements during the negotiations; the suit seeks a court order enforcing compliance with the statute and potentially invalidating actions taken in the allegedly improper sessions. This case is separate from Project Dazzler, a different $1 billion data center proposal also underway in Scioto County.

shortName: Sharp v. City of Wilmington
citation: Sharp v. City of Wilmington, Ohio
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio
category: Constitutional Law: Due Process
summary: Wilmington, Ohio residents Jessica and Logan Sharp, joined by neighboring property owners, sued the City of Wilmington (with Amazon Data Services later intervening as a defendant), challenging three city ordinances — rezoning a parcel, permitting data centers as a permitted land use, and regulating generator noise — that cleared the way for a roughly 471-acre, $4 billion Amazon Web Services data center campus near the Sharps' home. Plaintiffs allege the city violated Ohio's statutory public-notice requirements (which mandate 30 days' published notice and written notice to abutting property owners at least 20 days before zoning hearings) and their due process rights under the U.S. and Ohio Constitutions by failing to provide adequate notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard before passing the ordinances. Following a three-day evidentiary hearing, the federal court ruled on July 14, 2026 that the city's public notice for each of the three ordinances was seriously defective, and ordered that the city cannot act on the data center's site plan until it repeals, replaces, or otherwise properly re-enacts the challenged ordinances through a compliant process — one that gives residents the right to present expert testimony and cross-examine witnesses.

shortName: Eagan Capital, LLC v. City of Eagan
citation: Eagan Capital, LLC v. City of Eagan
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Eagan Capital, LLC, a data center owner, sued the City of Eagan, Minnesota after the city council adopted a one-year moratorium in February 2026 on new or expanded data center development involving more than 20 megawatts of electricity use within 500 feet of homes. Eagan Capital argues the city lacks legal authority to regulate electricity demand or impose the moratorium, contending that the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission has exclusive authority over electricity regulation in the state; the company seeks $50,000 in damages. The city has said it denied a related Interim Use Permit to Eagan Capital after finding the company had installed temporary chiller units without required permits, and states it intends to defend the moratorium.

citation: Blocktree Properties, LLC v. Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant County Washington
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: Blocktree Properties and several affiliated Bitcoin-mining/data-hosting LLCs and an individual sued Grant County's Public Utility District No. 2 and its commissioners, alleging the utility's rate structure for cryptocurrency-mining customers violated Washington ratemaking law and the Due Process and Privileges and Immunities Clauses of the Washington State Constitution. Plaintiffs, who operated mining facilities drawn to the district by its low-cost hydroelectric power, sought declaratory and injunctive relief and damages; the court denied a preliminary injunction in 2019 (affirmed by the Ninth Circuit on interlocutory appeal), and on March 12, 2020, granted summary judgment in the utility district's favor on all claims, closing the case.

shortName: Columbia Riverkeeper v. FERC
citation: Columbia Riverkeeper’s request for rehearing of order issuing original license and request for stay
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Columbia Riverkeeper petitioned the Ninth Circuit to review the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's issuance of an original hydroelectric license for the Goldendale pumped-storage energy project in Washington State, which would be built partly on Pushpum, a site sacred to the Yakama Nation, near the John Day Dam on the Columbia River. Columbia Riverkeeper argues the project — reported to be a major prospective power source for a nearby hyperscale data center campus proposed by STACK Infrastructure — will cause significant and unavoidable adverse impacts to Yakama cultural and historic resources, as separately found in a state environmental review; the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation filed a related, separate petition for review of the same FERC licensing decision.
