category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Citizens for Fauquier County, a conservation nonprofit, sued the Town of Warrenton in Fauquier County Circuit Court in December 2022 to compel disclosure of more than 3,100 emails concerning Amazon's proposal to build a 220,000-square-foot data center in the town, after the Town withheld the records under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act's "working papers" exemption for the mayor and town manager. The circuit court ruled the records could be withheld; the nonprofit appealed, and on July 30, 2024, the Virginia Court of Appeals reversed, holding the trial court had misapplied the "or" in the statutory exemption to shield both officials' correspondence.

shortName: Underwood Family Farm, LLC v. Prince William Cnty.
citation: Underwood Family Farm, LLC v. Prince William Cnty., No. CL24005849-00 (Prince William Cnty. Cir. Ct. Jan. 20, 2026) (denying motion for reconsideration of summary judgment granted to defendant).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Underwood Family Farm and other landowners in the Prince William Digital Gateway data center corridor sued the county in July 2024 over sharply higher real estate assessments after the December 2023 rezoning. They allege the county assessed their parcels based on speculative future use in combination with surrounding land they had not yet sold, that the assessments were arbitrary, capricious, and non-uniform, and that rollback taxes were improperly charged. They seek corrected assessments and refunds. A Prince William Times report describes a ruling by a circuit judge that the Pageland Lane land had in fact been rezoned for data centers even though the developers had not yet bought it, which the paper characterized as adverse to the landowners. The county has discounted the assessments by about 70%, and individual valuation trials could take up to two years.

shortName: Palmer v. Unified Government of Wyandotte Cnty. & Kansas City
citation: Neal H. Palmer, Et Al Vs. Unified Government Of Wyandotte County And Kansas City, Kansas
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Wyandotte County resident Neal Palmer and Haskell Farms LLC sued the Unified Government of Wyandotte County and Kansas City, Kansas, challenging its approval of zoning changes from residential to commercial use for a proposed $12 billion, six-building "hyperscale" data center campus by developer Red Wolf DCD Properties along Parallel Parkway. Plaintiffs allege the rezoning approvals contained "numerous errors and insufficiencies" that failed to comply with the Unified Government's municipal code, that the planning commission rushed its review without adequately studying short- and long-term impacts, and that a commissioner was improperly pressured to recuse himself from the hearings; they further allege the developer orchestrated an effort to have residents who had signed protest petitions withdraw their signatures to avoid a supermajority-approval requirement. On October 29, 2025, the court denied the Unified Government's motion to dismiss the claims regarding the south tract, while the claims about the north tract were allowed to proceed contingent on the commissioners reaching a "final decision" on that portion of the rezoning.

shortName: 1000 Friends of Oregon v. Dias
citation: 1000 Friends of Oregon, Kipperlyn Sinclair, Jacob Roloff, Tammy Carpenter, Aaron Nicholsetal. vs Dan Dias, Robby Hammond, City of Hillsboro, Eric Olson, Washington County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: 1000 Friends of Oregon and several individual and organizational co-petitioners filed a Petition for Writ of Review and Complaint for Declaratory and Injunctive Relief against City of Hillsboro officials (Dan Dias, Robby Hammond, City of Hillsboro) and Washington County officials (Eric Olson, Washington County), naming nine data center companies (including NTT Global, Adobe, QTS, CoreWeave, Dropbox, Flexential, and NVIDIA) as "opposite parties." Petitioners allege the City and County exceeded their jurisdiction, failed to follow statutory procedures, made findings unsupported by substantial evidence, and misconstrued Oregon's Enterprise Zone Act (ORS 285C) in approving a batch of Enterprise Zone tax exemption contracts and authorizations — some extending property tax breaks through 2051 — shortly before a new state moratorium (HB 4084) took effect. The petition seeks a writ of review reversing or annulling the challenged contracts and approvals, declaratory relief under Oregon's Uniform Declaratory Judgments Act, and an award of attorney fees.

shortName: Application of Xcel Energy and Otter Tail Power Company for an Energy Facility Permit to Construct the PowerOn Midwest Project
citation: Application of Xcel Energy and Otter Tail Power Company for an Energy Facility Permit to Construct the PowerOn Midwest Project, Docket No. EL26-026 (S.D. Pub. Utils. Comm'n, filed Sept. 4, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The South Dakota PUC is considering an application for a 160 miles of new 765 kv transmission lines and multiple substation upgrades from Excel energy called PowerOn Midwest. The need for the new high capacity backbone line is being justified by the applicant based on increasing demand from data centers and industrial projects. Some community members oppose the project and the PUC is currently considering requests for confidential documents to be shared with the public.

shortName: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC v. Bd. of Assessment Appeals
citation: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC v. Board of Assessment Appeals of Trumbull, 211 Conn. App. 559 (2022), cert. denied, 343 Conn. 926 (2022).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC, owner of a data center property at 60 Merritt Boulevard in Trumbull, Connecticut, brought a real estate tax appeal challenging the Town of Trumbull's property tax assessment, which the plaintiff alleged was grossly excessive (the town valued the property at roughly $15.2 million after Digital had purchased it for $45,000, and further imposed a 25% penalty for an allegedly late personal-property declaration). The trial court sustained Digital's appeals and ordered a reduction in the assessment, applying an income-capitalization approach to determine fair market value; the Town and its Board of Assessment Appeals appealed, arguing the trial court's valuation findings were clearly erroneous. The Appellate Court of Connecticut affirmed the trial court's judgment reducing the assessment.

The order covers visibility reporting (auditing), grid performance monitoring, ramp rate limits and ride-through requirements to avoid many loads dropping simultaneously. The filing is part of MISO's response to FERC's show-cause order from June 2026.

summary: West Buckeye Rd LP, owner of a 70-acre parcel at Buckeye Road and 99th Avenue, sued the City of Phoenix under Arizona's Proposition 207, which lets owners seek compensation when new land use rules reduce property value. The owner alleges Phoenix's 2025 ordinance restricting data center development, which it contends had previously been a permitted use, cut the property's fair market value by more than $54 million. It also estimates at least $9 million in costs to meet the new standards. The complaint states the city said in October 2025 that it was willing to negotiate but has neither paid compensation nor granted a waiver. The owner seeks a court order offsetting its lost value plus attorneys' fees.

category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The Decatur Township Civic Council and several individual property owners petitioned for judicial review of the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission's March 18, 2026 decision granting a "variance of use" allowing Sabey Data Center Properties LLC to build a roughly $4 billion, 130-acre, 250-megawatt data center campus. Petitioners allege the Commission and City-County Council approved the variance and related commitment modifications in violation of Indiana law and petitioners' due process rights, contending Sabey used a variance to bypass the formal rezoning process — which would have let the district's City-County Council representative "call down" the matter for a full council vote — and that the project conflicts with the area's approved mixed-use plan. The petition seeks to overturn the approval and, separately, requests an injunction to block construction while the case proceeds.

The complaint alleges NorthWestern has "stonewalled" the PSC's own requests for information about the data center agreements and improperly delayed seeking regulatory review until after contracts are executed, and asks the Commission to investigate NorthWestern's conduct and require greater transparency, including disclosure of the identities of data center applicants and the costs of any related transmission studies.

summary: Angelita Soriano and several other Hobart, Indiana residents sued the City of Hobart Plan Commission and the Hobart Common Council in Lake Superior Court, alleging the city violated their due process rights under the U.S. and Indiana constitutions when it rezoned roughly 725 acres of residential land to light-industrial use to accommodate a proposed Amazon data center. Plaintiffs contend the city's actions — including limiting public comment until after votes were taken — were "arbitrary, capricious," and unsupported by substantial evidence, and argue the project will diminish their property values and use and enjoyment of their homes. category: Corporate Tax, Securities, Employment and Lobbying: Employment
summary: Former safety managers Cheree Pace and Alton R. Matthews, along with other plaintiffs, sued general contractor HITT Contracting and related subcontractors over their termination from the QTS data center construction project in Fayetteville, Georgia, alleging wrongful termination, blacklisting, and retaliation for raising safety concerns. Plaintiffs allege that despite HITT and QTS's public "culture of care" messaging, qualified safety personnel were sidelined on site while undertrained supervisors were promoted, creating conditions plaintiffs say contributed to a June 2025 worker fatality; Pace alleges she was fired after being harassed and blamed for safety issues she tried to correct, while Matthews alleges he was terminated after requesting proof of operator certifications and that a fabricated harassment complaint was used against him. Defendants have sought to remove the case from Fayette County Superior Court to federal court, while plaintiffs — who state they have struggled to secure legal representation — have argued the retaliation and defamation claims are properly matters of Georgia state law.

summary: Layne Thornton and two Toledo Dairy business entities, whose farmland borders the proposed 620-acre "Gemstone Technology Park" data center site, filed a petition for judicial review challenging the Kuna City Council's April 2025 approval (by a 3-2 vote, with the mayor breaking the tie) of the project's rezoning. Petitioners alleged that council member Greg McPherson should have recused himself from the vote because he was employed by Thornton, creating an economic conflict of interest, and cited concerns about the project's traffic, power, water use, and environmental impact, including testimony that the data center's electricity demand could raise local power rates. The district court rejected the petition, finding Thornton had not shown a direct, particularized economic interest distinguishable from the broader community's interest in the project, and specifically held that potential power-rate increases were not a sufficiently direct impact; the petitioners have appealed that dismissal to the Idaho Supreme Court.

The PUC argues public disclosure of large Bitcoin-mining facilities' details could aid terrorist attacks on the state's electric grid and critical infrastructure, while the underlying AG ruling had found the commission failed to demonstrate the requested data identified specific vulnerabilities to terrorism.

summary: BladeRoom Group and an affiliate sued Facebook, Emerson Electric, and related Emerson entities in 2015, alleging that after BladeRoom pitched its modular data center design to Facebook under a non-disclosure agreement in 2011–2012, Facebook and Emerson conspired to misappropriate BladeRoom's trade secrets to build Facebook's Luleå, Sweden data center, and that Facebook then shared the design through the Open Compute Project without authorization. BladeRoom's claims included breach of the NDA, misappropriation of trade secrets, unjust enrichment, and unfair competition, and it originally sought roughly $365 million in damages. Facebook settled with BladeRoom during trial for a reported $365 million; the case proceeded to a jury verdict against Emerson alone, which found willful and malicious trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract and awarded roughly $30 million in compensatory damages (later increased with exemplary damages and prejudgment interest to over $77 million) — a judgment the Ninth Circuit later vacated in part on appeal, remanding for further proceedings regarding the NDA's expiration date.

summary: RD Michigan Property Owner I LLC (an affiliate of developer Related Digital) and the site's landowners sued Saline Township two days after its Board of Trustees voted 4-1 on September 10, 2025 to deny rezoning 575 acres of farmland from agricultural to industrial for the "Saline Barn" data center project (planned to serve OpenAI and Oracle as part of the "Stargate" AI infrastructure initiative). Plaintiffs alleged the township engaged in unconstitutional "exclusionary zoning" under Michigan law by having no land zoned to permit data center use anywhere in the township, rendering the denial arbitrary given that a data center qualified as a legitimate land use the community could not categorically exclude. The township settled and a county judge certified the settlement in October 2025, allowing construction to proceed in exchange for roughly $14 million in community benefit payments from the developer; a separate resident's later motion to intervene in the settlement, alleging the township's decision to settle itself violated the Michigan Open Meetings Act, was denied by the court.

summary: Thor Equities sued the City of Urbana, its city council, and its Building and Zoning Appeals Board in June 2026 over a proposed roughly $1 billion data center campus on about 230 acres. Thor alleges the city violated state and local law when it reversed course after enabling the project. It says the city annexed and rezoned the land in April 2025 to allow data centers, approved a tax abatement agreement in November 2025, and then rejected its February 2026 site plan. The city also adopted a 12-month moratorium in March 2026 and repealed the data center zoning in June 2026. Thor says it has spent about $19.6 million and seeks to preserve its ability to build the project.

KIA alleges the moratorium was enacted specifically to block its already-pending project and unlawfully halted development after it had invested more than $2 million assembling and preparing the land, and separately alleges the Planning Commission failed to process its development plan application. summary:
1778 Rich Pike LLC appealed the Clifton Township Zoning Hearing Board's November 19, 2025 decision to the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas. The Board had denied the developer's substantive validity challenge to the township's zoning ordinance, which the developer argued excluded data center uses. The appeal contends that data center uses are legitimate land uses entitled to zoning accommodation under state law, that the ordinance fails to define or classify data center uses and is therefore exclusionary, that the ordinance lacks any comparable use to which data centers could be analogized, and that it provides no reasonable path to approval by special exception.

category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: This is a regulatory rate proceeding rather than adversarial litigation. Evergy applied to the Kansas Corporation Commission (KCC) in February 2025 for approval of a new Large Load Power Service (LLPS) rate plan designed for electric customers — primarily data centers and large manufacturers — requiring 75 megawatts or more of peak power, in order to recover the incremental cost of serving such customers without shifting those costs to existing ratepayers. On November 6, 2025, the KCC approved a unanimous settlement reached among Evergy, KCC Staff, the Citizens' Utility Ratepayer Board, industrial-consumer and data-center industry groups (including Google and the Data Center Coalition), and conservation organizations (including the Sierra Club), establishing minimum contract terms of 12 to 17 years (with up to a five-year ramp-up period), direct assignment of large-load-specific system upgrade costs to the new customer, and incentives for large-load customers that help fund or generate their own clean energy.

citation: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, Inc. v. City of Franklin Planning and Zoning Commission, et al.
corporateEntities: Tenkey Landco I, LLC; SPDJ Partners, LLC; OTN Development Company, LLC; “Project Lionsgate/Blackjack”
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, a local nonprofit, sued the City of Franklin Planning and Zoning Commission and developer entities (Tenkey Landco I, LLC, SPDJ Partners, LLC, and OTN Development Company, LLC) behind a proposed AI data center campus with on-site power generation on roughly 200 acres near I-65 (referred to as "Project Lionsgate/Blackjack"). Plaintiffs allege the Commission's March 2026 unanimous approval of a preliminary development plan for the project was arbitrary, capricious, and inconsistent with the City of Franklin Zoning Ordinance, because the Commission had previously rejected a proposed zoning text amendment that would have explicitly allowed data centers and on-site power generation, and had indicated any such project would instead require a conditional-use permit — which only the Franklin Board of Adjustments can grant. The suit also raises concerns about noise, light pollution, air emissions, and strain on local water resources, and asks the court to overturn the preliminary plan approval. This is the second of two related lawsuits over the project; in the other, the developer (TenKey) is separately suing Simpson County over a conditional-use-permit ordinance the company says gives the county excessive control over the project.

The underlying case involves the Indiana Utilities Regulatory Commission's approval of two gas plants proposed by Duke Energy under a pay-as-you build approach.  Citizens Action Coalition and Vote Solar challenged the decision in court and Duke responded by petitioning the Indiana Supreme Court to rule on the associational standing issue.

shortName: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg Cnty. v. Valara Holdings, LLC
citation: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg Cnty. v. Valara Holdings, LLC, No. 2026-CP-42-03416 (S.C. Ct. Com. Pl. dismissed Oct. 6, 2026), appeal docketed (S.C. Ct. App. filed Oct. 20, 2026).
forum: Spartanburg County Court of Common Pleas
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County, represented by the South Carolina Environmental Law Center, sued Valara Holdings LLC and Spartanburg County, alleging that a roughly $2.8–3 billion data center project on the former Kohler industrial site was improperly classified and approved as a "minor land development" under the county's Unified Land Management Ordinance — a designation that bypassed the public review process (planning commission review, public notice, hearings, and a public vote) required for "major" developments. Plaintiffs contend the developer split the project into two applications to keep each under the minor-development threshold, despite the combined project's scale, and point to a much smaller industrial facility that was separately classified as "major," while raising concerns about water quality, air emissions from an associated natural gas power plant, and the ordinance's protective purpose. The suit asks the court to require the county to conduct the major-development public review process; a hearing was scheduled for July 30, 2026.

summary: Daniel Piatt and other Granbury, Texas residents sued the City of Granbury and city officials after the city council voted April 7, 2026 to rezone a 2,100-acre parcel ("Knox Ranch") backed by Bilateral Energy for a potential data center project known as "Project Patriot." Plaintiffs allege the annexation of the land, completed in January 2026, was marked by procedural violations, including that officials failed to properly disclose the annexation's connection to the data center plans, and that city officials violated the Texas Open Meetings Act by deliberately staggering their arrival times during a tour of a Bilateral Energy facility in Dallas to avoid triggering the Act's quorum and public-notice requirements (an alleged "walking quorum"). The suit seeks a pause on further action related to the data center, revocation of the annexation, and damages.

category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: TenKey LandCo I, LLC, the applicant for a roughly $1.6 billion, three-building data center with on-site natural gas generation ("Project Lionsgate/Blackjack") on Steele Road in Franklin, Kentucky, sued the Simpson County Fiscal Court in January 2026. It challenges a December 2025 county ordinance that limits data centers and integrated energy systems to heavy-industrial zones, requires a conditional use permit, and applies inside city limits as well as in unincorporated areas. TenKey argues the county lacks authority under Kentucky's planning statutes to regulate a project located entirely within Franklin, which has its own planning and zoning commission. It seeks a declaratory judgment that the ordinance is invalid or unenforceable within city limits. The county has since passed an updated version of the ordinance, and the court heard arguments on the ordinance's legality in August 2026.

shortName: Guido v. Columbia Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Gregory Guido, Jr. v. Columbia County Board Of Commissioners
corporateEntities: White Oak Business Center; Pumpkin Center
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Gregory Paul Guido Jr., a Harlem, Georgia resident, filed petitions for judicial review challenging the Columbia County Board of Commissioners' February 2026 approvals rezoning the White Oak Business Center and Pumpkin Center properties to Data Center District zoning for two large data center campuses. Guido alleges the county approved the rezonings without a verified water-usage or sewer-capacity analysis required by the county's Water and Sewer Division, relied on a stale traffic study prepared for an earlier version of the White Oak project, and failed to analyze the impacts of shifting the project's primary access point. The Superior Court dismissed all of Guido's related petitions (including a separate one concerning a nearby quarry) with prejudice; Guido moved for reconsideration, arguing the dismissal order failed to address the facts pled, improperly treated the distinct cases as one, and wrongly required land ownership (rather than proximity and demonstrable harm, which he argues is the correct standard under Georgia law) to establish standing. The matter is now before the Georgia Court of Appeals.

shortName: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City, the Cave City Council and the Joint City-County Planning Commission
citation: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City, the Cave City Council and the Joint City-County Planning Commission
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: In a second, related lawsuit, Kentucky Industrial Alliance (KIA) asked the Barren County Circuit Court to void Cave City's September 2024 annexation (Ordinance 24-9-9C) of the approximately 245-acre former Branstetter property where KIA's data center project is planned — arguing that if the annexation is invalid, the property would fall outside city jurisdiction and the city's data center moratorium (challenged in the companion case above) would not apply to it. KIA's complaint centers on a roughly 0.09-acre parcel containing the historic Shaw Cemetery within the annexed tract, alleging that Branstetter Family Holdings did not actually own the cemetery parcel (whose title traces to a 1902 deed) when it signed consent to the annexation, and that KIA — not Branstetter — was declared the cemetery's rightful successor-in-title by a December 2024 default judgment in unrelated litigation; KIA contends the entire annexation ordinance must be invalidated, rather than just the cemetery parcel excised from it, because the city intended to annex one unified site. This case has been consolidated with KIA's earlier moratorium challenge, with the annexation issue proceeding first since it could resolve the city's jurisdiction over the property entirely.

summary: GenOn applied to FERC under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act for approval to sell its shuttered, roughly 1,260-megawatt Morgantown power plant in Maryland (four oil-fired units retired in 2022) to TeraWulf, a Bitcoin-mining company pivoting toward data centers. PJM's independent market monitor, Monitoring Analytics, urged FERC on March 4, 2026 to reject the deal, arguing that removing the Morgantown units from PJM's wholesale market to serve TeraWulf's planned data center load would be inconsistent with the public interest and would shift costs and risks to other PJM customers, particularly since the plant sits in a transmission-constrained zone. TeraWulf disputes this characterization, stating it intends to build roughly 500 MW of new gas generation and 250 MW of battery storage in each of two phases — positioning itself as a net electricity generator for the state rather than a net consumer — while consumer advocacy group Public Citizen has separately asked FERC to require TeraWulf to detail its plans for remediating legacy coal pollution at the site.

summary: Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy, and the Sierra Club (with Friends of Blackwater joining one appeal) appealed the state's air permit for Fundamental Data's proposed Ridgeline natural gas power plant and data center near Thomas and Davis, West Virginia. The other challenges the handling of the draft permit and the company's confidentiality claims over redacted materials. Petitioners contend the plant, planned at 750 megawatts or more, is improperly treated as a minor source. In August 2026 the court dismissed both appeals on jurisdictional grounds without reaching the merits. It held the final-permit appeal belongs in the state Supreme Court, and it found no jurisdiction over the draft-permit appeal, calling it moot. After negotiation, Appalachian Power, Google, and a group representing West Virginia manufacturers reached a settlement — later subject to Commission approval — setting minimum contract terms for large-load customers, including a 100 MW minimum capacity per site, a minimum 12-year initial contract term, and a requirement to commit to purchasing at least 80% of expected power consumption.

shortName: Switch, Ltd. v. NVLCO Storey Cnty., LLC

forum: United States District Court for the District of Nevada
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Switch, Ltd. sued data center developer Tract (through affiliate NVLCO Storey County) over the scope of a restrictive covenant negotiated in 2015 between Switch and the original landowner of the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center, seeking a broad interpretation that would bar Tract from developing single-tenant, cloud, or hyperscale data centers — not just multi-tenant facilities — on the "Peru Shelf" parcels Tract now owns. Tract argued the covenant's plain, unambiguous language restricts only multi-tenant data center facilities, consistent with Switch's own business model at the time the covenant was negotiated. A related Nevada state court (First Judicial District, Storey County) entered final judgment in October 2025 in Tract's favor on all of Switch's claims, holding the covenant restricts only multi-tenant facilities and does not extend to single-tenant, cloud, or hyperscale data centers serving one customer, closing more than two years of litigation; this federal docket may reflect a related or removed proceeding and should be checked against the state court record for its specific procedural relationship to that judgment.

shortName: Greenidge Generation LLC v. New York State Dep't of Environmental Conservation
citation: Greenidge Generation LLC vs. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation et al
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Greenidge Generation, operator of a natural gas power plant and Bitcoin-mining data center in Dresden, New York, sued the state Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) after DEC denied renewal of the facility's Clean Air Act Title V operating permit, and later moved to force the plant's closure. Greenidge alleged DEC lacked authority under New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) to deny the permit based on a determination that continued operation would be inconsistent with statewide greenhouse-gas limits, and that DEC misapplied the CLCPA by failing to assess whether a justification or mitigation measures existed for the denial. On November 14, 2024, the Yates County Supreme Court annulled DEC's permit denial, holding that while the CLCPA authorizes such denials, the agency's discretion is limited and must rest on proper analysis; DEC appealed, but the parties later settled, with DEC agreeing to issue Greenidge a new five-year Title V permit incorporating emissions reductions, and the appeal was discontinued by stipulation in late 2025.

category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: Georgia Interfaith Power & Light, Park Avenue Baptist Church, the Unitarian Universalist Church of Savannah, the Sierra Club (and its Georgia Chapter Director Adrien Webber, individually), and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy — represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Sierra Club — petitioned the Fulton County Superior Court to review the Georgia Public Service Commission's December 2025 decision approving Georgia Power's plan to add roughly 10 gigawatts of new electric generation, including expensive new gas units at Plant McIntosh, largely to serve anticipated data center demand. Petitioners allege the Commission violated Georgia law by approving the buildout without properly demonstrating the new capacity is actually needed — noting that some of the demand is speculative and tied to data centers that have not signed contracts with Georgia Power — and argue the decision will leave "captive" ratepayers responsible for an estimated $50–60 billion in costs over coming decades. The petition asks the court to send the approval back to the Commission for reconsideration.

shortName: People v. DOE
citation: People of the State of Michigan v. DOE
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: The People of the State of Michigan, joined by the states of Minnesota and Illinois and several environmental organizations (including Sierra Club, NRDC, and the Environmental Defense Fund), petitioned for review of a May 23, 2025 U.S. Department of Energy order issued under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, which compelled Consumers Energy to keep its J.H. Campbell coal-fired plant in West Olive, Michigan running past its scheduled May 31, 2025 retirement date by declaring a regional energy emergency. Petitioners argued the Michigan Public Service Commission and grid operator MISO had already approved retiring and replacing the plant after finding it was not needed for reliability, and that DOE's order improperly overrode state and utility planning processes without evidence of a genuine emergency, at a cost the petitioners said would total hundreds of millions of dollars in higher electricity bills across the region. The D.C. Circuit ultimately vacated the DOE order, holding that Section 202(c) functions as a narrow emergency backstop rather than a mechanism for overriding established state, utility, and regional grid-planning processes.

shortName: Virginia Electric and Power Company - For approval of a Certificates of Public Convenience and Necessity to construct/operate the proposed Chesterfield Energy and approval of designated Rider CERC
citation: In re Virginia Electric and Power Company (Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center and Rider CERC)
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: Dominion Energy applied to the SCC for a certificate of public convenience and necessity to build the Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center. This is a 944-megawatt gas peaker plant costing about $1.47 billion, to be sited at a former coal plant near the James River, with cost recovery through a designated rider. The SCC approved the project in November 2025. Appalachian Voices, Mothers Out Front, and the Chesterfield County NAACP branch petitioned for reconsideration, arguing the plant would violate the Virginia Clean Economy Act and impose environmental injustice on nearby communities. In early 2026 the SCC denied reconsideration, finding the reliability need placed the plant in the public interest, that it did not violate the Act's gas-retirement mandate, and that the state's air-quality analysis was reasonable. The groups, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, then appealed the separate state air permit in Richmond Circuit Court.

shortName: Hatfield v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
citation: Hatfield v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Ten southern West Virginia residents sued the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and project developer TransGas Development Systems over the proposed Adams Fork Energy project — a 117-engine, self-contained "micro-grid" power plant and ammonia facility intended to include associated data centers near Wharncliffe on the Mingo-Logan county line. Plaintiffs allege the project would violate the Endangered Species Act (threatening the endangered Guyandotte Crayfish, threatened Big Sandy Crayfish, and endangered Gray Bat and Northern long-eared bat), the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the Natural Gas Act, because the federal defendants have not conducted required environmental consultation, review, or permitting despite the state having already issued an air-emissions construction permit for what plaintiffs say is legally a "major source" of air pollution. Plaintiffs sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary and permanent injunctions barring further construction activity until all required federal reviews are completed.

summary: The Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the Safe and Sound Coalition, the NAACP, and Young, Gifted & Green, petitioned the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality for an evidentiary hearing to challenge the state permit board's March 2026 approval of an air permit authorizing 41 new, permanent gas turbines at xAI's Southaven data center facility. Petitioners argue the permit's air-quality modeling failed to demonstrate that pollution from the turbines — which would emit substantial nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, and formaldehyde — would not further degrade air quality in an area already failing to meet federal ambient air quality standards, and that the approval process denied the public meaningful opportunity for input; MDEQ maintains its modeling shows the turbines would keep the area in compliance with national standards.

shortName: In re Ohio Power Co.
citation: In the Matter of the Application of Ohio Power Company for New Tariffs Related to Data Centers and Mobile Data Centers
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: American Electric Power (AEP) Ohio applied to the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) for a new tariff specifically governing data centers and other large-load customers, after AEP reported more than 50 data centers in its interconnection queue representing over 30,000 megawatts of additional demand and had paused new data center service requests in 2023 pending a framework. In July 2025, the PUCO approved a negotiated version of AEP's proposed tariff requiring data center customers to pay for at least 85% of their stated power needs regardless of actual usage, sign minimum 12-year contracts, and pay exit fees equal to three years of minimum charges if they leave early — terms AEP says are needed to prevent stranded infrastructure costs from falling on other ratepayers. The Ohio Manufacturers' Association has separately appealed this approval (and PUCO's earlier sanctioning of AEP's data-center service moratorium) to the Ohio Supreme Court, arguing the tariff unlawfully discriminates against a specific customer class.

shortName: Amazon Data Services, Inc. v. PacifiCorp
citation: Amazon Data Services, Inc. vs PacifiCorp, d/b/a Pacific Power,
category: Energy Law: State PUC
summary: Amazon Data Services filed a complaint with the Oregon Public Utility Commission against PacifiCorp (d/b/a Pacific Power), a Berkshire Hathaway-owned utility, alleging PacifiCorp has failed since 2021 to meet its obligations to supply adequate electric power to Amazon Web Services data center campuses in Oregon. The complaint states that one AWS campus has insufficient power, a second has none at all, and PacifiCorp has refused to complete standard contracting for two additional planned campuses. The proceeding seeks Commission intervention to compel adequate service, though the specific relief requested in the complaint was not detailed in available reporting.

documents.title: Complaint
documents.description: Amazon Data Services alleges PacifiCorp failed to deliver contracted power to four Oregon data center campuses and improperly demanded a 32.6 percent tax gross-up, and asks the Commission to compel service or remove the sites from PacifiCorp's exclusive service territory.

shortName: We Are Mason Cnty., KY, Inc. v. Mason Cnty.
citation: We Are Mason County, KY, Inc. v. Mason County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: We Are Mason County, a local nonprofit opposing a proposed hyperscale data center complex near Maysville, sued the Mason County Fiscal Court and the joint planning commission. The group argues the ordinance and approvals allowing the project are contrary to the county's comprehensive plan, which does not address where or how many data centers may be built. In May 2026 the Fiscal Court rezoned 28 properties totaling about 2,080 acres for rural industrial use for an undisclosed AI company. A second complaint filed in July 2026 by the group and individual residents challenges that rezoning. It alleges the comprehensive plan should have been amended first and that the rezoning lacked substantial evidence. Both suits ask the court to reverse the county's actions.

shortName: State ex rel. Bristolville 25 Developer LLC v. Village of Lordstown
citation: The State of Ohio ex rel. Bristolville 25 Developer LLC v. Vill. of Lordstown, No. 2025-1497 (Ohio Sup. Ct. filed Nov. 12, 2025)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Bristolville 25 Developer LLC and property owner BHGH Properties LLC filed an original mandamus action in November 2025 against the Village of Lordstown and its zoning administrator. They seek to compel the village to accept and review their October 20, 2025 site plan for a $3.6 billion, roughly 133-acre data center campus. The developers argue data centers were a permitted use when they applied, and that the village refused to process the plan while council considered a data center ban that passed on November 3, 2025. The village denies improperly blocking the project and says the ban has since been repealed, though it later adopted a moratorium. In December 2025 the court dismissed the village solicitor as a party, denied dismissal as to the village and zoning administrator, and granted an alternative writ that moved the case to the evidence stage.

shortName: City of Imperial v. Cnty. of Imperial
citation: City of Imperial vs. County of Imperial et al
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The City of Imperial sued Imperial County and its Board of Supervisors, along with developer Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC and Dubose Design Group, Inc., over the county's approval of a nearly 1-million-square-foot AI data center complex at Aten and Clark roads. The city alleges the county improperly classified a required grading permit as "ministerial" — an administrative act requiring no discretionary review — to bypass the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), and contends the project instead required rezoning and a conditional use permit given its scale. The city sought an immediate injunction halting grading and construction pending resolution; in February 2026 the court ruled the city's amended complaint did not, as pleaded, state a legally sufficient cause of action.

shortName: State of California v. Wright
citation: State of California v. Wright
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of California
category: Constitutional Law: Separation of Powers
summary: California and twelve other states (along with California's Governor's Office of Business and Economic Development) sued U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, the Department of Energy, and the Office of Management and Budget, alleging the administration unlawfully terminated federal funding for energy and infrastructure programs established under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and Inflation Reduction Act — including roughly $1.2 billion in funding for California's ARCHES clean-hydrogen hub and funding for Washington's Pacific Northwest Hydrogen Hub. Plaintiffs allege the terminations, based on a May 2025 DOE policy memorandum, exceeded executive authority, violated the constitutional separation of powers by overriding congressionally appropriated funds, and were arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act; they seek declaratory and injunctive relief restoring the funding.

shortName: FX Solutions v. Broad Reach Power, LLC
citation: FX Solutions v. Encap., et al.
corporateEntities: FX Solutions; Encap; Quantica; Broad Reach Power; Engie
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: FX Solutions and its principal, Montana businessman Rick Tabish, sued Broad Reach Power, LLC, its Texas private-equity owner EnCap, and successor entity Quantica Infrastructure, alleging breach of contract, breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing, tortious interference, and unjust enrichment arising from a soured deal involving land near a NorthWestern Energy substation in Broadview, Montana. FX alleges it sold 350 acres surrounding the substation to Broad Reach Power in reliance on a promise that Broad Reach would supply power (at roughly $24 per megawatt-hour, well below market rates) to run FX's planned data center, but that Broad Reach — secretly directed by EnCap — never intended to deliver the power and instead transferred its energy assets to the newly formed Quantica, which is now building its own data center on the land FX sold, using a separate agreement with NorthWestern for up to 1 gigawatt of power. The defendants deny any binding power-purchase contract existed, characterizing the arrangement as an unenforceable "agreement to agree," and argue Broad Reach Power has since been dissolved; FX seeks unspecified damages.

shortName: Great Lakes Neighbors, Inc. v. City of Port Washington Joint Review Bd.
citation: Great Lakes Neighbors, Inc. v. City of Port Washington Joint Review Board et al
corporateEntities: Vantage Data Center "Lighthouse"; Open AI; Oracle
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Great Lakes Neighbors Inc. sued the City of Port Washington and its Joint Review Board, seeking to void a $458 million tax incremental financing (TIF) district the city approved in November 2025 to fund infrastructure for Vantage Data Center's "Lighthouse" campus (part of the OpenAI/Oracle "Stargate" program). The suit alleges the district fails Wisconsin's statutory requirements — that at least half the property be blighted or qualify as industrial land, and that the project pass the "but-for" test showing it would not proceed without TIF support — and further alleges the city improperly agreed to reimburse the developer for costs (including interest payments) not allowed under the TIF statute, and that officials may have violated the state's Open Meetings law during related discussions. The suit asks the court to declare the TIF district invalid.

shortName: PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,070 (2025).
citation: PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,070 (2025).
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: This is a FERC-initiated regulatory proceeding rather than adversarial litigation. Following a February 2025 show-cause order, FERC issued a final order on December 18, 2025 finding that PJM Interconnection's transmission tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it fails to clearly address the rates, terms, and conditions of service for large loads — including AI-driven data centers — that co-locate directly with electric generating facilities. FERC directed PJM to propose new tariff provisions establishing three transmission-service options reflecting how co-located loads draw from the grid (an interim non-firm service and new Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand services), to revise its behind-the-meter generation rules to properly account for co-located loads in resource-adequacy planning, and to report on the reliability impacts of data centers and other large-load customers; FERC set a compliance and paper-hearing schedule running from January through April 2026 for interested stakeholders to weigh in on the final rates and terms.
